sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Go's testing package is built into the standard library and the `go test` command is part of the toolchain — no external framework needed. Interviewers ask about testing because it signals whether a fresher can contribute to a real team codebase from day one. The table-driven test pattern, the distinction between `t.Error` and `t.Fatal`, and knowing how to run and filter tests are all questions that come up in Go fresher interviews.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body:
Three conventions that make Go testing work:

- **The `_test.go` suffix is magic.** Files ending in `_test.go` are only compiled when running `go test`. The test binary is a separate executable. You can have both unit tests (same package) and black-box tests (package with `_test` suffix) in the same directory.
- **Test functions follow a naming contract, not a base class.** `TestAdd(t *testing.T)` — starts with `Test`, takes `*testing.T`, returns nothing. No `@Test` annotation, no extending TestCase. The naming convention is the contract.
- **Table-driven tests are the idiomatic Go pattern.** A slice of `struct{ input, expected }` test cases with a single `for _, tc := range tests` loop. This is standard in the Go standard library itself and what interviewers expect to see.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- **Test file naming** — file must end in `_test.go`; package can be `package foo` (whitebox) or `package foo_test` (blackbox); both can coexist
- **testing.T basics** — `t.Logf("msg: %v", v)` logs (shown with -v); `t.Errorf("got %v, want %v", got, want)` marks test failed but continues; `t.Fatalf(...)` marks failed and stops immediately
- **t.Error vs t.Fatal** — `t.Error/t.Errorf` continues running the test after reporting failure; `t.Fatal/t.Fatalf` stops the test immediately (like return); use Fatal when subsequent assertions depend on a prior one passing
- **Table-driven tests** — `tests := []struct{ name, input string; want int }{ {"empty", "", 0}, {"one", "a", 1} }; for _, tc := range tests { t.Run(tc.name, func(t *testing.T) { ... }) }`
- **Running tests** — `go test ./...` runs all tests; `go test -v ./...` verbose; `go test -run TestName` runs matching tests; `go test -count=1` disables test caching
- **Test coverage** — `go test -cover ./...` prints coverage percentage; `go test -coverprofile=coverage.out; go tool cover -html=coverage.out` for HTML report
- **Example functions** — `func ExampleAdd() { fmt.Println(Add(1,2)) // Output: 3 }` — compiled and run as tests; output comment is the expected stdout

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- **`t.Fatal` inside a goroutine panics** — calling `t.Fatal` from inside a goroutine spawned by the test (not the main test goroutine) panics the test binary. Use `t.Error` and a `sync.WaitGroup` for concurrent test assertions.
- **`t.Run` creates a subtest** — table-driven tests should use `t.Run(tc.name, func(t *testing.T) {...})` not just a bare loop. `t.Run` makes failures identifiable by name and supports parallel subtests with `t.Parallel()`.
- **`-count=1` to force re-run** — `go test` caches results and will not re-run unchanged tests. `go test -count=1 ./...` forces a fresh run. Interviewers ask: 'why does go test sometimes not run your tests?'
- **Test file in the same package vs `_test` package** — `package foo_test` tests only the exported API (blackbox); `package foo` can access unexported symbols (whitebox). Both are valid; blackbox is preferred for testing public contracts.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: > *"In Go, tests live in `_test.go` files and follow the `TestXxx(t *testing.T)` naming convention — no framework needed. I use `t.Errorf` to report a failure and continue running, and `t.Fatalf` to stop immediately when subsequent assertions would not be meaningful. For covering multiple cases, I write table-driven tests: a slice of struct test cases with a `for _, tc := range tests { t.Run(tc.name, ...) }` loop. I run tests with `go test -race -cover ./...` to catch races and measure coverage at the same time."*
